case: Improve Chrome for heavy users, a classic product exercise. The first draft follows a public walkthrough by IGotAnOffer on YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XAJeXlY6w-c); the answers, and frames 3, 6, 7 and the assumptions, are a reconstruction

fields.decision: Which Chrome improvement to build first, for people who work all day in the browser
fields.how_to_read: Left to right. Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 follow the presenter's answer in the video, in our own words. Step 3, the test and metrics in step 6, step 7 and the assumptions are reconstructed for this example. Yellow stamp: the review changed it.

frames.name: Goal

draft.question: Is this the goal, or is there one above it?
draft.proposal: Raise user satisfaction, because Chrome already has the market share and the risk is losing users, not finding them.

fields.business_goal: Keep heavy users satisfied so they do not switch browsers
fields.user_problem: People who work all day in Chrome lose time and focus juggling tabs

frames.answer: Satisfaction, yes. Acquisition, engagement and revenue were weighed and set aside with a reason.

final.business_goal: Keep heavy users satisfied so they do not switch browsers
final.user_problem: People who work all day in Chrome lose time and focus juggling tabs
final.metric: Satisfaction score (CSAT) of heavy users, chosen over NPS because few people recommend a browser
final.why_now: Chrome already leads in share, and rival browsers compete on features (assumption)
final.brief_and_givens: Open brief: how would you improve Chrome? No data, about 25 minutes, one reviewer.

frames.name: Customer

draft.question: Why this customer and not the other?
draft.proposal: Heavy users, because every small change weighs most for them.

segments.name: Heavy user, a knowledge worker in the browser all day

fields.chosen_why: Small changes weigh most for them

frames.answer: Heavy users. Light users matter for acquisition, and acquisition is not the goal.

final.chosen_why: A knowledge worker in the browser all day. We assume heavy users are about 20% of users and most of the time spent; small changes weigh most for them, and light users matter for acquisition, which is not the goal

frames.name: Their moment and what they use it for

draft.question: Is this scene real? What does she want underneath?
draft.proposal: The presenter's own day as a heavy Chrome user.

fields.persona: The presenter himself, a heavy Chrome user
fields.moment: Any workday with many tabs open

frames.answer: Not you: name a user of the segment and tell her day. It works here only because the presenter is in the segment.
frames.change: From the presenter's own experience to a named user of the segment, with a concrete scene.

final.persona: Maya, a sales analyst who keeps 30 or more tabs open all day (invented for this example)
final.moment: Two minutes before a client call, she needs the deal sheet she opened this morning and cannot find its tab
final.deeper_want: To feel in control of her day instead of chasing windows
use_cases: Get back to a document she already opened (priority)
Open a Drive file she has not opened today
Join her next meeting on time
final.prioritized_use_case: Get back to a document she already opened

frames.name: Where it fails today

draft.question: These, or is one missing?
draft.proposal: Memory and battery drain, and productivity. Productivity first.

failures.name: Finding the right tab
failures.cause: With many tabs only the icons show
failures.alternative_today: Scans tabs one by one, or opens Drive and searches again, four or five steps

failures.name: Late to meetings
failures.cause: The calendar is one more tab
failures.alternative_today: Keeps the calendar tab open and checks it

failures.name: Tab overload
failures.cause: Tabs pile up and nobody closes them

failures.name: Memory and battery drain
failures.alternative_today: Closes tabs or restarts the browser

fields.ranking_criterion: Time lost per day, and how many heavy users hit it

frames.answer: Those, with productivity first. Memory and battery stay on the list, out of scope for now.

frames.name: Ideas

draft.question: Which one would you add?
draft.proposal: Three ideas of different size, one per failure.

ideas.name: Meeting alert with the join link
One shortcut that searches open tabs, Drive and history
Tabs that sort and clean themselves

frames.answer: These three. Each one closes with its impact in one line.

ideas.name: Meeting alert with the join link
One shortcut that searches open tabs, Drive and history
Tabs that sort and clean themselves

final.scoring: Time saved, reach, ease of building, 1 to 5 (our scores, from the reasoning in the video): search 5, 5, 4 · meeting alert 3, 2, 4 · smart tabs 2, 5, 2

frames.name: Choose, hypothesis and metrics

draft.question: Is this the idea that moves the goal most, and is this how we would know?
draft.proposal: Universal search: it saves the most time, reaches the most users and Google already knows search.

fields.chosen_idea: One shortcut that searches open tabs, Drive and history
fields.why_vs_goal: Saves the most time for the most heavy users, at a reasonable cost

frames.answer: Good pick. Before building, say how we would know it worked and how to test it small.
frames.change: Added the hypothesis with baseline, target and timeframe, the metrics, a cheap test and the weak spot: the video ends at the pick.

final.chosen_idea: One shortcut that searches open tabs, Drive and history
final.why_vs_goal: Saves the most time for the most heavy users, at a reasonable cost, and time saved is what moves their satisfaction

hypothesis.statement: One shortcut to any open tab, Drive file or past page gets heavy users to the right document faster

metrics.primary: Median time from intent to the right document
metrics.secondary: Share of heavy users who use the shortcut every week
metrics.guardrails: Memory use and page load do not get worse

final.cheap_test: Ship the shortcut over open tabs only, to 1% of heavy users, before indexing Drive
final.weak_spot: Searching Drive means touching the user's files: privacy and speed decide it

frames.name: Growth and vision

draft.question: What is left out?
draft.proposal: Three phases, from open tabs to every file the user works with.

fields.growth: The shortcut becomes a habit on every computer the user signs into
phases: Plus Drive and other work files
fields.company_strategy_fit: Chrome as the front door to search and to the user's work files
fields.dilemma_principle: When features and speed pull apart, the browser stays fast
fields.one_sentence_summary: For people who work all day in Chrome, one shortcut that finds any tab, file or past page, measured by how fast they reach the right document

frames.answer: Nothing to add. Meeting alerts and smart tabs wait for the next round.

final.growth: The shortcut becomes a habit on every computer the user signs into
phases: Plus Drive and other work files

frames.name: Assumptions

draft.question: Which one worries you most?
draft.proposal: That users will let Chrome search their files.

assumptions: Heavy users are about 20% of users and most of the time spent
Finding the right tab costs heavy users minutes every day
Today it takes about 40 s to reach a document that is already open
Users will let Chrome search their Drive
fields.most_worrying: Users will let Chrome search their Drive

frames.answer: The Drive one. If people do not trust it, the search stays at tabs and history.
